svg.text: C1-B TOP EXIT — window in the top wall, lift-and-slide hatch (recommended)
The box leaves upward through a lined window in the appliance top; one insulated slide seals it like a door.
hatch open 3.4 s per passage, 1 small motor
per opening: fridge 0.2 kJ, freezer 0.5 kJ
ZOOM: top of the fridge (front section)
OPEN: WHERE THE COLD AIR GOES
opening in a side or door
CLOSED: WHY THE HATCH MUST PRESS SHUT
room air pushed in at the top
cold air leaks out at the bottom
tall cold column: 1.1–2.6 Pa at the top
so the slide presses onto a magnetic gasket
(compression, like a door), never a sliding
or brush seal: in a freezer that would grow
about 13 kg of ice a year in the seal.
Freezer: 3 W heated seat, 100 mm skirt

g.text: 1/7 Inside the fridge the in-cell mechanism (S1 stacks) puts the wanted box on the port stack under the throat. The hatch stays shut.
2/7 A small motor pulls the slide: ramps lift it 4 mm off its magnetic gasket, then it slides 260 mm aside.
3/7 The gallery hoist reaches about 190 mm down through the throat, grips the box and lifts it out.
4/7 A constant-force spring pulls the slide back onto the gasket: open only 3.4 s, and it shuts by itself on power loss.
5/7 Cold air is heavy and stays in the cell: a top hatch lets out only about the box's own volume (5–10 L); a side opening spills 37–58 L.
6/7 Closed, the tall cold cell pushes cold air out at the bottom and sucks room air in at the top: the hatch must seal by pressing.
7/7 Put-away is the same in reverse. The OEM door, controller and refrigerant circuit stay untouched; the door is the service door.
